answer:
Nowadays it is more or less impossible to avoid English if you lead a normal life. You hear it on TV and in song lyrics, you study it at school, and for many people it is part of their everyday work. This constant contact with the language gives you a fairly good sense of how it should be used. I think most people understand at least some English, and quite a few probably master it very well. However, when I look at my own abilities, it is quite clear that some areas are more problematic than others. I find myself more confident with the more passive skills — reading and listening — whereas writing and speaking are the more difficult areas.

Throughout the years I have studied English, first at primary school and then at upper secondary school, my teachers have always emphasised writing. In upper secondary school in particular we wrote a great many essays of various kinds, as well as reviews. But even though I have had a fair amount of practice in writing English, there are still problems. Spelling can, of course, sometimes be difficult, but a worse problem, from my point of view, is that of grammatical errors. In my experience these problems are often complicated and not as easy to come to terms with as, for example, the spelling of a word, which you can easily look up in a dictionary.

When it came to reading, we did not get very much practice at school. We did, of course, have textbooks, but the articles in them were often very short, each one covering a different topic, which gave the impression that they had been taken out of context. In other words, the textbooks were boring. Besides these texts we also read a number of literary works, on which we wrote reviews. I think reading actual literature is an enormously rewarding way of learning to use a language more fluently. I benefited greatly from this as well when I studied religious studies, since much of the literature on those courses was in English.

The most serious problem I have when reading English texts arises when they are written in professional or academic language. To read an English text that would probably cause trouble even in Swedish is a real challenge, and at the same time very time-consuming. This also brings to mind another problem with my reading, namely my patience, or rather my lack of it. Naturally, reading an English text is a slower process than reading a Swedish one, at least to begin with, but for some reason I find that hard to accept.

The two skills of speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Even so, I think listening is the easiest of the four skills, while speaking is the most difficult. This undoubtedly has to do with the fact that you automatically get far more practice in listening, especially from TV and music, than in speaking. You do not, of course, understand every word, but usually you have no trouble grasping the context. In spite of this, the problem of professional language arises in listening as well as in reading.

As I said above, my biggest problem with English has to do with speaking. I have had no real experience of speaking English, since I have never been abroad for any length of time. And since the teaching of English at school is based primarily, or even exclusively, on theory, I have had no practice there either. If anything, school makes you want to talk even less: you become so hung up on getting everything grammatically correct that you do not dare open your mouth, for fear of being laughed at. I know that sounds terrible, and it probably does not apply to everyone, but on the other hand I believe such fears disappear quite quickly once you actually start talking.

Having completed this assignment, I have to say that it is really hard to judge oneself in the four skills of a language. I have never had any trouble getting good grades in English at school, but then again I firmly believe that grades rarely say anything about someone's actual knowledge. All I know is that there are many different areas to a language, and I would like to improve my knowledge in all of them.
